result:
I’ve been thinking about thresholds lately.

Not the big, dramatic turning points in life — not graduations or moves or heartbreaks — but the actual, physical thresholds. The quiet in-between places.

Doorways. Coastlines. Dusk. The moment before you fall asleep when you’re not quite awake and not quite dreaming. The three seconds after someone tells a joke but before everyone laughs.

We don’t really *live* in thresholds. We pass through them. We’re always on our way to somewhere else, so we forget to notice them. But I think thresholds are where most of life actually happens.

Take dusk. It’s not day. It’s not night. Light is doing this impossible thing where it has no source anymore — it’s just *in the air*. Everything looks softer, like the world has taken its armor off. People speak a little quieter at dusk without knowing why. Photographers call it the golden hour, but it feels more like the honest hour. Things aren’t hiding in bright sun or in darkness. They just are.

Or coastlines. My favorite kind of map to look at is not a political map, but a topographical one where you can see where the ocean gets deep. That jagged, fractal border between land and sea is never the same twice. The tide comes in and erases it. The tide goes out and redraws it. The land is trying to hold its shape and the sea is trying to remind it that nothing holds its shape forever. And standing there, with your feet in the wet sand, you are literally standing on an argument between two worlds that has been going on for four billion years.

And then there are the human thresholds — the ones we create.

Waiting rooms. Train platforms at 11pm. Airports at 5am. Kitchens during a party, where two people who don’t know each other end up having the most real conversation of the night while leaning against a refrigerator.

Elevators. The way strangers instantly agree to a temporary social contract: stare at the numbers, don’t make eye contact, pretend you’re alone together.

Even conversations have thresholds. That pause after someone says something vulnerable. You can feel the air change. You can either rush to fill it with words, or you can let it sit there and become a doorway. If you let it sit, the other person will often walk through it and tell you something true.

I think we’re nostalgic for thresholds because they give us permission to not be one thing yet. You don’t have to be the person you were before you walked through the door, and you don’t have to be the person you’ll be after. For a second, you’re just *potential*.

Maybe that’s why I like writing. A blank page is a threshold. It’s not empty. It’s full of everything it *could* become. And the moment you write the first sentence, you collapse all that potential into one reality. Which is sad, but also beautiful. Because you actually made something exist that didn’t before.

We spend so much energy trying to be certain, to be solid, to be defined. But solid things crack. Fluid things adapt.

I want to get better at lingering in the doorway instead of rushing through it.

So that’s what I wanted to write about today — the places that are nowhere and everywhere.

What kind of thresholds have you been standing in lately?
